Q: Power BI Python Visualization erroring out when it shouldn't A:

Your guess in the question was right, and your comment has the other half.

sm.OLS needs numeric input. sm.add_constant(df['Category']) on a string column produces an object dtype frame, and the fit fails when it coerces to float.

The 150k limit explains why it looked backwards. Starting at 2011 puts you over the cap, so Power BI truncates. The rows that survived were the early ones, where category names were all numeric. Narrowing the range drops you under the cap, so the alphabetic names come through and OLS fails.

That also means the 2011 chart was wrong. It fit an OLS on an arbitrary subset of 150k rows.

Let statsmodels encode the categorical:

import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model = smf.ols('Value ~ C(Category)', data=df).fit()
df['Fitted'] = model.fittedvalues

C() marks the column as categorical. On the array API, use pd.get_dummies(df['Category'], drop_first=True, dtype=float) before add_constant. Pandas 2.x returns bools without dtype=float.

Q: How do I see the commit differences between branches in git? A:

To see all the commits like what you gonna see in "Commits" tab of your PR, run these:

1. Basic:

git log --oneline origin/base..origin/my-branch

2. If you don't want branches/tags, add --no-decorate

git log --oneline --no-decorate origin/base..origin/my-branch

3. If you want to sort commits chronologically (oldest first), add --reverse

git log --oneline --no-decorate --reverse origin/base..origin/my-branch

Q: What is a good design for custom extensions to a Java class? A:

The subclass thing isn't really a subclass problem, it's this line:

extensions.put(extension.getClass(), extension);

You're deriving the key from the value. Everything else follows from that. The runtime class isn't necessarily the class the caller thinks they're storing, and once you've stored it you can't recover what they meant. Both other answers fix it by making the caller pass the key, and at that point there's nothing left to resolve, because you're not inferring anything.

I'd take Louis's Key<T> over Class<T>, for a reason that matters specifically to you as a library author rather than to a single application: Class is a shared namespace.

Two unrelated consumers of your library who both reach for String.class will silently clobber each other, and neither has any way of knowing the other exists. An identity-based Key is owned by whoever declares it, so that can't happen.

Q: npm install failing with error "error Build failed with error code: 1" A:

error gyp ERR! node-gyp -v v3.8.0

For python v3.x please upgrade node-gyp to a version greater than 5.0.5: https://github.com/nodejs/node-gyp/releases

See:

  • https://github.com/nodejs/node-gyp/issues/1687
  • https://github.com/nodejs/node-gyp/issues/1337 (slim-hmidi has the same error)

Q: Compiling and parsing After Effects JavaScript code A:

All features available through Javascript are listed in the doc: After Effects Scripting Guide

There's no way to actually compile it, and there's no official way to run the script from outside After Effects, even though a very limited CLI is available.
(a C++ API is available though)

What I've found after lots of tests is a bit hacky but proved reliable, using the aerender CLI, originally made for background rendering:

1. Copy your .jsx into one of the startup scripts location of After Effects (there's one in the folder where After Effects is installed (with admin rights), and one in the "appdata" location (with standard user rights); these paths depend on the OS (Windows or Mac OS) and can be found from within After Effects; in the settings there's a button to open the settings location where user scripts are located too.
2. Run arender with an empty, fake project. This starts a full background instance of After Effects thus runs the startup scripts, which then have access to all features of After Effects, can even load and save projects, etc. When the scripts are finished, After Effects would then continue with opening the empty project and fail at rendering, but the scripts have been run anyway before that.
3. You can then delete your .jsx file from the startup scripts folder.

I can't have a look at the paths and more details for now as I'm on Linux, but I know for sure this works well and it's the only way I've found so far (after 15 years of working with this kind of stuff) to run scripts from a third-party app or the command line, which then have access at the full JS API, as a background task without UI.
